question: According to current official Bun documentation, how can Bun.WebView connect to an already-running browser over a browser-level CDP WebSocket URL, and which lifecycle operations are documented?

claims.text: Bun documents connecting `Bun.WebView` to an already-running browser by using `backend: { type: "chrome", url: "ws://..." }`, described as connecting to a specific DevTools WebSocket URL.
acceptable_patterns: Connect to a specific DevTools WebSocket URL

evidence_passages.text: To make `Bun.WebView` connect to an already-running browser over a CDP WebSocket, Bun documents the `backend` object form with `type: "chrome"` and a `url` field set to a `ws://...` DevTools endpoint; the example shown is `ws://127.0.0.1:9222/devtools/browser/abc123...`. The docs say this is how to “Connect to a specific DevTools WebSocket URL.”

claims.text: Bun also documents an auto-connect path: before spawning Chrome, it checks `DevToolsActivePort` in standard profile directories and, if it finds a running browser with remote debugging enabled, connects over WebSocket instead of spawning a new browser.
acceptable_patterns: connects? over WebSocket instead of spawning

evidence_passages.text: Bun also documents an auto-connect path: before spawning Chrome, it checks `DevToolsActivePort` in standard profile directories, and if it finds a running browser with remote debugging enabled, it connects over WebSocket instead of spawning a new browser.

claims.text: To make a running Chrome connectable this way, the docs say to enable remote debugging via `chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging` or by launching Chrome with `--remote-debugging-port=9222`.

evidence_passages.text: To enable that remote debugging on a running Chrome, the docs say to either use `chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging` and enable the toggle, or launch Chrome with `--remote-debugging-port=9222`.

claims.text: For `view.close()`, the docs say closing is synchronous and idempotent, destroys the page's renderer process, rejects pending promises on that view with `Error("WebView closed")`, and later method calls throw `ERR_INVALID_STATE`; `Symbol.dispose` and `Symbol.asyncDispose` both point to `close()`.

evidence_passages.text: For `view.close()`, the docs say closing is synchronous and idempotent, destroys the page’s renderer process, rejects pending promises on that view with `Error("WebView closed")`, and makes later method calls throw `ERR_INVALID_STATE`. They also say `Symbol.dispose` and `Symbol.asyncDispose` both point to `close()`, so `using` and `await using` perform automatic cleanup.

claims.text: For `Bun.WebView.closeAll()`, the docs say it force-kills the Chrome subprocess and the WebKit host subprocess with `SIGKILL`, causes pending promises on every view to reject on the next event-loop tick, allows later `new Bun.WebView()` calls to respawn browsers as needed, and is called automatically at process exit.

evidence_passages.text: For `Bun.WebView.closeAll()`, the docs say it force-kills the Chrome subprocess and the WebKit host subprocess with `SIGKILL`, causes pending promises on every view to reject on the next event-loop tick, and allows later `new Bun.WebView()` calls to respawn browsers as needed. The docs also say Bun calls `closeAll()` automatically at process exit.

rejected_claims.text: The docs explicitly call the `ws://127.0.0.1:9222/devtools/browser/abc123...` example a browser-level CDP WebSocket URL.
rejected_claims.reason: The evidence supports the example path and DevTools WebSocket wording, but says the browser-level label is an inference rather than text explicitly defined in the docs.
One evidence passage lists these as methods, but the stronger and more specific evidence says the explicitly documented lifecycle operations are only `view.close()` and `Bun.WebView.closeAll()`.

rejected_claims.text: An explicit `backend.url` works for non-`ws://` schemes or for tab-level `devtools/page/...` endpoints.
rejected_claims.reason: No supplied evidence supports non-`ws://` schemes or tab-level endpoint forms.

rejected_claims.text: The docs specify different `close()` or `closeAll()` behavior when Bun attaches to an already-running browser instead of spawning one.
rejected_claims.reason: The supplied evidence does not document attach-specific lifecycle differences.

rejected_claims.text: The docs state that `url: false` disables auto-detect and forces Bun to spawn a fresh headless Chrome, while an explicit `url: "ws://..."` does not fall back to spawning if the connection fails and instead throws.
rejected_claims.reason: Claim composite dont seule la partie `url: false` (« skip auto-detect ») est corroborée par un extrait fetché. Le « forces Bun to spawn a fresh headless Chrome » et le « does not fall back to spawning… instead, it throws » ne reposent que sur la reformulation auto-générée du run Codex (aucune opened_url) et durcissent une preuve contradictoire : l'extrait WebFetch de bun.com/docs/runtime/webview indique au contraire « the WebSocket connect fails and Bun transparently falls back to spawning its own Chrome ».

rejected_claims.text: The docs further state that `path` or `argv` imply spawn mode, skip auto-detect, and cannot be combined with `url: "ws://..."`.
rejected_claims.reason: Aucun extrait de documentation récupéré ne mentionne `path` ni `argv`, ni la contrainte d'incompatibilité avec `url: "ws://..."`. Assertion présente uniquement dans la reformulation Codex sans citation d'ancrage : risque de fait inventé, non vérifiable à partir des preuves fournies.

rejected_claims.text: The explicitly documented lifecycle operations are `view.close()` and `Bun.WebView.closeAll()`.
rejected_claims.reason: L'exhaustivité affirmée (les opérations de cycle de vie documentées « sont » close() et closeAll()) est directement contredite par l'extrait WebFetch de la même page, qui liste sous « Lifecycle methods/operations » : navigate(url), goBack(), goForward(), reload(), close(), Symbol.dispose/asyncDispose et WebView.closeAll(). De plus, le pattern « explicitly documented lifecycle operations » impose une tournure de prose spécifique, trop étroite pour une notation lexicale fiable.
